lines.text: This scrap was hidden in a tiny pocket inside a dead man's trousers.
Two words. Tamam Shud. Persian for, ended.
Somerton Beach, Adelaide. The first of December, 1948.
A well-dressed man, dead against the seawall. No ID.
The labels on his clothes had been cut out.
Weeks later, a suitcase linked to him turned up at Adelaide railway station.
Its label? Removed too.
Then someone handed police the very book that scrap was torn from.
The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam.
On the back cover, in pencil: a phone number, and lines of letters.
A code. Nobody has ever cracked it.
Cause of death? Never determined. Poison was suspected. None was found.
Spy. Lost love. Suicide. Plenty of theories, no proof.
Then, in 2021, police exhumed his body.
In 2022, a professor and a genealogist tested hairs from his plaster death mask.
The DNA led through family trees to a name.
Carl, Charles, Webb. An electrical engineer from Melbourne, born 1905.
But it isn't official. Police and the coroner haven't confirmed it yet.
And even if he is Webb, no one knows how he died.
Or what the code says.
So what do you think those letters spell?
It all comes back to this.
